title: Kheer Bhawani's spring
hookLine: a bowl of rice pudding set down beside a spring, for a goddess who lives in the water
carry: Kheer Bhawani: the Mother is fed like family
tomorrow: why soak walnuts in pots of water all night for Shiva?
last: PRATYABHIJNA: RECOGNIZE THE SHIVA ALREADY HERE.

cards: A bowl of rice pudding, cooked slowly in milk, carried in two hands down a path under tall trees. At the end of the path there's a spring, and in the middle of the spring, a small shrine.

People bend at the edge of the water and offer the pudding, kheer, and milk, and flowers. Then they do something you might not expect at a temple. They look down, carefully, at the color of the water.
Why bring pudding to a goddess, and why read her water?

teach.b: The shrine stands in a village called Tulmul, not far from Srinagar.
The goddess there is called Ragnya, or Maharagnya, a form of the Mother. She also goes by a homelier name: Kheer Bhawani, Bhawani of the rice pudding, because of what her devotees bring her.
Bhawani is a name of the Goddess, the wife of Shiva, so the name holds the kitchen and the heavens together. That's the teaching inside the name.
Many Hindus come to the Goddess as Ma, Mother, and you bring a mother food from your own kitchen.
The offering is called naivedya. Once she has received it, it comes back as prasad, her blessing, to be eaten. It's why so many Hindu homes set the first portion aside for God before anyone eats.

The shrine sits in the water, and the water matters too. Tradition says the spring changes color: pilgrims say clear, light shades are a good sign, and dark shades have been read as a warning of hard times for the valley.

teach.h: A FESTIVAL THAT IS A HOMECOMING
teach.b: Some take that as a plain wonder; others hear a community that keeps watching the same water together, year after year. The goddess of Tulmul is especially dear to Kashmiri Pandits, the Hindu community of the valley.
Her festival day is kept as a homecoming, and families who now live far from Kashmir still try to come back to the spring for it, carrying milk and pudding the way their grandparents did.
A temple can be a place you visit. This one is also a mother's house you return to.

how: At the Kheer Bhawani shrine at Tulmul, near Srinagar, devotees offer kheer, milk and flowers at the spring around the shrine, and Kashmiri Pandit families gather there on the goddess's festival day.

games.q: Nani makes kheer for a puja and won't let anyone taste it until it's been offered. your little cousin is starving. what's the reason?

games.why: it's naivedya: the Mother is fed first, like family. then the kheer comes back as prasad, and your cousin gets a bowl.

practice: Before your next meal, set a small first portion aside, a spoonful on a clean plate, the way many Hindu homes offer naivedya before eating. If you have a shrine, place it there and say the Goddess's name, Bhawani, once.
If you don't pray, set it aside with thanks for whoever cooked. Afterward, eat it, or share it.

wordCard.voice: Kashmir. Today, the spring at Tulmul, where Kheer Bhawani sits in the water, people bring her rice pudding, and pilgrims read the water's color. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a name of the Goddess, the wife of Shiva; at Tulmul she's Kheer Bhawani, Bhawani of the rice pudding.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: Kheer Bhawani, the Mother fed like family. At Tulmul a community brings her kheer, and comes home to her. Rest well.
